quote: Die Frage ob eine geg. Funktion $f(x, y, z)$ von $x, y, z$ sich nach [-3fa-] $n\ (=3)$ maliger Anwendung [-(3)-] von [-Fun-] geeigneten Funktion von nur 2 Argumenten erzeugen [-(3)-] lässt
english: The question whether a given function f(x, y, z) of x, y, z can be generated by n (=3)-fold application of suitable functions of only 2 arguments
topic: Hilbert derives the partial differential equations satisfied by functions obtained by repeatedly composing functions of only two arguments with functions of x, y, z, and reduces the question of whether a given f(x,y,z) can be so generated after n (=3) steps to the solvability of a system of partial differential equations.

triage.modern_statement: Take the class C_n of (locally) analytic functions of x, y, z that you can build in n nested steps, where each step applies an arbitrary function of two arguments to x, y, z or to functions built earlier. Example: f = F(G(x,y), H(y,z)). Question: given f(x,y,z), how do you decide whether f is in C_n (here n = 3)? Hilbert's approach is to eliminate the arbitrary two-variable functions, which gives a system of partial differential equations (differential-algebraic conditions) satisfied by every member of C_n. The question then becomes whether f satisfies that system or whether the system is solvable. In modern language, this asks for a differential-algebraic description of the depth-n superposition classes. It is the analytic, depth-limited version of Hilbert's 13th problem, and today it is studied under the name 'analytic complexity'.
triage.answered_by: This is part of the circle of Hilbert's 13th problem (ICM 1900). Several results followed. Kolmogorov (1956) and Arnold (1957) settled the continuous version positively: every continuous function can be written as a superposition of continuous functions of two variables, and even of one variable plus addition. Vitushkin (1954, 1964) settled the smooth (differentiable) version negatively. For analytic functions, it is easy to show that some analytic f(x,y,z) is not a superposition of analytic functions of two variables. The specific idea in this note was later made systematic by V. K. Beloshapka's 'analytic complexity' (2007 onward). He showed that each class of functions of complexity at most n is a differential-algebraic set, cut out by differential polynomials, and gave an algorithm to produce those polynomials. He treated two variables first and several variables in 2016. Later work, e.g. by Sadykov and coauthors, gives algorithms for checking membership in the second class. The algebraic-function version of the 13th problem is still open.

evidence.claim: In 1957 Kolmogorov and Arnold solved Hilbert's 13th problem, which asks whether continuous functions of several variables are superpositions of continuous functions of fewer variables. Vitushkin solved the finitely differentiable version in 1964.
For each n there is a polynomial that is not an n-times nested superposition of infinitely differentiable functions of two variables. This shows that depth-limited superposition classes are proper.

Vitushkin's survey says it is easy to show that some analytic function of three variables is not a superposition of analytic functions of two variables. It also says the algebraic form of the problem remains open.

Beloshapka (2007) defined analytic complexity and proved that the class of functions of a given complexity is a differential-algebraic set. He also described an algorithm for obtaining the relations that define each class.

For each analytic complexity class Cl_n there is a system of differential polynomials that annihilates a function exactly when the function belongs to Cl_n. Computing these polynomials has very high computational complexity.
Research is ongoing, e.g. an algorithm to check whether a bivariate analytic function belongs to the second analytic complexity class.

triage.why: The note asks whether a given f(x,y,z) arises from a fixed number of nested applications of two-variable functions, and turns this into the solvability of partial differential equations. That is exactly the setting of Hilbert's 13th problem; in the published problem Hilbert claimed analytic functions of three variables exist that cannot be built this way. The continuous and smooth versions were settled by Kolmogorov–Arnold and Vitushkin. The PDE (differential-algebraic) characterization of fixed-depth analytic superpositions was developed as Beloshapka's 'analytic complexity' theory, which is still being worked on.
